passages.t: The siege drawn on a brick
passages.happening:
God tells Ezekiel to take a brick, draw Jerusalem on it, and lay siege to it, with a siege wall, a ramp, camps and battering rams (verses 1-2). He is to set up an iron plate as a wall between himself and the city, and turn his face against it. ‘This will be a sign to the house of Israel’ (verse 3).

Then he is to lie on his left side for 390 days and bear the iniquity of the house of Israel, and on his right side for 40 days for the house of Judah, ‘a day for each year’ (verses 4-6). He is to face the siege with his arm bared and prophesy, and God will bind him so that he cannot turn until the days are finished (verses 7-8).
passages.hearers:
These were standard siege methods. Attackers surrounded a city to cut off food and escape, built an earth ramp up to the wall, and brought battering rams up the ramp. Assyrian reliefs of the siege of Lachish in 701 BC show these tactics, and Babylon used them against Jerusalem.

Clay bricks were Babylonia's building material and were also used for writing and drawing, so sketching a city on one was natural. The iron plate was probably a flat griddle for baking, turned into a picture of a wall between God and the city.

The 390 and 40 days are hard to explain. The number 390 has been counted from the division of the kingdom or from the building of the temple, or read as a time of punishment still ahead. Forty is a generation, as in the wilderness. The Greek translation reads 190 instead of 390. No explanation has won agreement; the text says only that each day stands for a year.
passages.later: The Babylonians built siege works around Jerusalem, and famine gripped the city (2 Kings 25:1-3). In the wilderness, Israel bore its guilt forty years, ‘a year for each day’ (Numbers 14:34).
passages.hard:
Did Ezekiel really lie on his side for over a year, and why would God command something so strange?

The text says the actions were commanded and done in the people's sight, but not exactly how. Some take it literally: Ezekiel lay on his side for part of each day over many days, rising to prepare food and see to other needs, which the chapter itself implies (verses 9-12). Others think the actions were done in a shortened or symbolic form, or that some were seen in vision. Attempts to explain his binding and silence as an illness read far more into the text than it gives, and are not widely accepted.

The sign-acts had a purpose. Words alone had not moved the exiles. A prophet living out the siege day after day made the coming disaster impossible to ignore. The prophet's body became a message because the people's ears were closed.
passages.asks: Ezekiel's whole life became a message. Ask what your daily habits say about what you believe. And ask whether you would be willing to look foolish for the sake of telling the truth.

passages.happening:
For the days he lies on his side, Ezekiel is to make bread from mixed grains, wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet and spelt, and eat a small weighed ration at set times, with a small measure of water (verses 9-11). He is to bake it over human dung in the people's sight. ‘This is how the Israelites will eat their defiled bread among the nations to which I will banish them’ (verse 13).

Ezekiel protests, ‘I have never defiled myself’ (verse 14). God lets him use cow dung instead (verse 15). Then he explains: he is going to cut off the food supply in Jerusalem, and its people will eat bread by weight and drink water by measure, and waste away in their iniquity (verses 16-17).
passages.hearers:
The mixed grains suggest scraping together whatever food is left, the kind of loaf made in scarcity. The ration was small, often estimated at around eight ounces of food a day and well under a liter of water.

Dried animal dung was a common cooking fuel where wood was scarce. Human waste, however, was unclean under Israel's law, which required it to be buried outside the camp. Ezekiel was a priest who had kept the purity laws all his life, and his protest is the cry of a man asked to defile himself. God's concession shows mercy to the prophet while keeping the sign: in exile, the people would eat unclean food.
passages.later: The law told Israel to go outside the camp and cover its waste (Deuteronomy 23:12-13). Lamentations grieves the famine of Jerusalem's siege (Lamentations 4:9-10).
passages.asks: God heard Ezekiel's protest and changed the command. Ask whether you bring your honest objections to God. And ask what it means that he listened to his servant.
